# Media

<p class="lede">Puts a figure beside a block of text and stacks them when the text would drop below half the width; the one-class form of a sidebar holding a frame and a stack.</p>

## Example

## When to use it

A comment with an avatar, a product with its thumbnail, a speaker with a headshot: whenever a picture sits beside a few lines of text, this is the shape. It stays side by side while the text keeps at least half the width and stacks when it cannot. Put the picture first for picture-left, last for picture-right; the reading order follows. The figure is whatever the reset counts as a picture: an `img`, `video`, `picture`, `canvas` or inline `svg`, bare or inside one wrapper, so a mark drawn in the page sits beside its text like a photograph. The body must not have any of those as a direct child (it would be taken for a second figure); an inline `svg` icon in the body goes beside its heading in a paragraph, or in a wrapper of its own.

`data-width` is the figure's width, and so where the two stack: a smaller figure holds the row down to a narrower window. On a wide row that leaves the text running long, so `data-max` caps the text from the width scale and the figure takes the rest. `<article class="media" data-width="sm" data-max="md">` stays side by side down to a phone and still keeps a reading measure at full width. The text's half of the row wins over the cap.

## Built from primitives

A recipe is a shortcut, not a new idea. The same result is three layouts you already know: a `sidebar` whose first child is a `frame` and whose second is a `stack`. Reach for this form when you want to change any part of it, since every knob is an attribute you can see.

```html
<div class="sidebar" data-width="sm">
	<div class="frame" data-ratio="1/1">
		<img src="ada.jpg" alt="Portrait of Ada Lovelace">
	</div>
	<div class="stack" data-gap="sm">
		<h3>Ada Lovelace</h3>
		<p>Wrote the first published algorithm, for Babbage's Analytical Engine.</p>
	</div>
</div>
```

The one-class form renders the same geometry, and its test proves it. Its attributes are the ones the primitives take. Its CSS is its own file, so a project that prefers the composed form can leave `css/recipes/media/media.css` out of a hand-built bundle. One difference: the sidebar's `data-side` picks which child is the sidebar, while the recipe's `data-side` reverses the row, which changes where the figure sits beside the text but not where it is read, and does nothing once the two have stacked.

## Why this name

Nicole Sullivan named the media object in 2010 and the name stuck across a decade of frameworks, Foundation 6's `.media-object` included. One word of it is enough.

| `data-max` | enum | `3xs`, `2xs`, `xs`, `sm`, `md`, `lg`, `xl`, `2xl` |  | The widest the text may run side by side; the figure takes the rest of a wide row. data-width still sets where the two stack. |
| `data-side` | enum | `start`, `end` |  | Put the figure at the start or the end while side by side, regardless of source order. Stacked, the source order holds. |

## Children

- `> *`: exactly 2. Exactly two: the figure (an img, video, picture, canvas or svg, or an element wrapping one) and the body; the body must not have any of those as a direct child (it would be taken for a second figure), so an inline svg icon inside the body goes in a wrapper or beside its heading in a paragraph. A figure with a figcaption keeps its caption below the picture.

## Accessibility

- The figure is cropped to its ratio, so alt text should describe what is visible. data-side changes where the figure sits, not where it is read.

## Browser support

- Used without guards: flexbox gap, aspect-ratio, object-fit, :has()
- Behind `@supports`: nothing

## JavaScript

None. This component is CSS only.

Available since 7.0.0.
